title: Do Hangover Pills Actually Work? What the Evidence Shows
excerpt: What the research shows about DHM, Blowfish, ZBiotics, Myrkl, prickly pear, Korean hangover pills and charcoal, ranked by the strength of the human evidence.
metaDescription: Do hangover pills work? What the research says about DHM, Blowfish, ZBiotics, Myrkl, prickly pear, Korean pills and charcoal, ranked by evidence.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
Mostly no. Two systematic reviews of the research, in 2005 and 2022, found no strong evidence that any pill, supplement or drug prevents or cures a hangover, and nothing on the shelf comes close to drinking less. That doesn't make every product useless. Aspirin-based pills such as Blowfish do ease a headache, at some risk to a stomach alcohol has already irritated. DHM, prickly pear extract and a few plant extracts used in Korean hangover drinks have small human studies or animal research suggesting they might take the edge off some symptoms. Activated charcoal and most "detox" blends have nothing worth the name behind them.

Below, the main categories are sorted by how strong the human evidence is, with links to our full review of each product.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes published research and product labels. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Hangover supplements are sold as dietary supplements, which means the FDA does not review them for safety or effectiveness before they go on sale. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before trying a hangover product if** you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have liver, kidney, or stomach problems, take blood thinners, antidepressants, diabetes medicine, or any regular prescription, or have been told to avoid aspirin or NSAIDs. **Get medical help right away** if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, or has blue-tinged or very pale skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no pill helps with that. In the US, call 911.

## Why Hangovers Are So Hard to Treat With a Pill

A hangover is several things going wrong at once, and researchers still argue about which matter most.

Acetaldehyde is the toxic first by-product of breaking down alcohol in the liver. Most people clear it fairly quickly, and since symptoms often peak after blood alcohol has fallen to zero, it's unclear how much it contributes to the morning itself.

Inflammation probably accounts for the achy, flu-like feeling; studies have found changes in immune signaling molecules called cytokines after heavy drinking. Sleep is another big part. Alcohol helps you fall asleep but breaks up the second half of the night, and much of the next-day fog may simply be sleep loss.

Alcohol also makes you urinate more and irritates the stomach lining, which adds thirst, headache and nausea, though dehydration alone doesn't explain how bad hangovers feel. Darker drinks like bourbon and red wine contain more congeners, by-products of fermentation that seem to make hangovers worse for some people. And as alcohol wears off, the brain's GABA and glutamate systems rebound, which may explain the jittery, anxious feeling some people get.

A pill aimed at one of these can only help with part of the problem, and nothing on the market has been shown to deal with all of them. You can read more about the underlying biology in our [complete hangover science hub](/never-hungover/complete-hangover-science-hub-2025).

## What the Big Research Reviews Found

The strongest evidence on whether something works comes from systematic reviews, which gather every good-quality trial on a question and read them together. Two have looked at hangover remedies.

In 2005, Pittler, Verster and Ernst reviewed the randomized trials of hangover treatments in the *BMJ* and concluded there was no compelling evidence that any conventional or complementary intervention prevented or treated hangovers.

In 2022, a team led from King's College London revisited the question in the journal *Addiction* with the newer trials. It found that a few substances, including clove extract, tolfenamic acid (an anti-inflammatory drug), pyritinol, Hovenia dulcis fruit extract, L-cysteine, red ginseng, and Korean pear juice, showed some improvement in individual studies. But the authors rated the quality of that evidence as very low. Most trials were small, many were run on young men, several were funded by manufacturers, and few results had been repeated by independent teams. Their conclusion was that no hangover remedy could be recommended with confidence.

Keep that in mind for every product below. When a brand says its formula is "clinically studied," it usually means one ingredient appeared in one small study, often at a different dose, sometimes in animals.

## The Main Types of Hangover Pills, Ranked by Evidence

"Evidence" in this table means published research in people, not marketing claims or customer reviews.

| Category | Examples | What it's supposed to do | Strength of evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Painkiller-based | Blowfish (aspirin + caffeine) | Ease headache and fatigue | Good for headache relief; real safety caveats with alcohol |
| DHM supplements | No Days Wasted, Double Wood, Flyby, Cheers | Support alcohol metabolism, reduce next-day symptoms | Promising animal research; limited human data |
| Prickly pear | Standalone or in blends | Reduce inflammation-related symptoms | One small human trial showed partial benefit |
| Korean and Japanese hangover products | Condition, Dawn 808, Ukon no Chikara | Plant extracts like Hovenia dulcis and turmeric | A few small studies; very low quality |
| Probiotic "pre-drink" products | ZBiotics, Myrkl | Break down alcohol or acetaldehyde in the gut | Plausible idea; mostly company-funded research |
| Vitamin and electrolyte blends | B-vitamin "morning after" packs | Replace nutrients, support hydration | Weak for hangovers specifically |
| Activated charcoal | Charcoal capsules | "Absorb" alcohol and toxins | Poor; charcoal binds alcohol badly |

## Painkiller-Based Pills: They Work, But Know What You're Taking

The hangover pills with the most reliable short-term effect are the ones that contain an actual drug. [Blowfish](/never-hungover/blowfish-hangover-review) is an over-the-counter tablet that combines aspirin with caffeine, the same pairing found in many standard headache tablets. Aspirin eases a pounding head and caffeine blunts grogginess, so people do feel better, and not only from placebo.

The catch is that you're taking an NSAID (a type of anti-inflammatory painkiller) on a stomach that alcohol has already irritated. The aspirin label in the US carries a warning about stomach bleeding for people who have three or more drinks a day. Aspirin also thins the blood, so it isn't suitable for people on blood thinners, people with ulcers, or anyone told to avoid it. Caffeine can worsen dehydration slightly and make jitteriness or anxiety worse.

A few practical rules if you choose this route:

- Take it the morning after, with food and water, not before bed while alcohol is still in your system.
- Don't stack it with other painkillers that contain aspirin or ibuprofen.
- Remember that it treats symptoms. It does nothing for the underlying causes of the hangover.

If you're weighing up painkillers in general, our guides on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explain the stomach and liver risks of each. For acetaminophen (Tylenol) one rule matters most: don't take it to "head off" a hangover, because alcohol and acetaminophen together can stress the liver.

## DHM Supplements: The Most Interesting Science, Still Early

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound, mostly extracted from vine tea and also found in the Japanese raisin tree, Hovenia dulcis. It's the main active ingredient in many Western hangover supplements, including No Days Wasted, Double Wood, Flyby and Cheers Restore.

Researchers took an interest after a 2012 paper in the *Journal of Neuroscience* by Shen and colleagues at UCLA. In rats, DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal, apparently by acting on GABA receptors in the brain, the same system alcohol affects. Later lab and animal studies suggested it may help the liver process alcohol and its by-products. A small 2015 randomized trial in people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease reported improvements in some liver markers, which is encouraging for the liver but says nothing about hangovers.

Very few well-designed human trials have looked at DHM and hangover symptoms directly, and most of what supplement websites say extrapolates from rats. Nobody has shown how well it works in people, at what dose, or for whom. There is no established human dose; products range from 300 mg to 1,000 mg a serving.

Of the hangover ingredients, DHM has the most plausible mechanism and the most active research, and it has been well tolerated in the studies that exist. It's a reasonable thing to try if you expect a modest effect or none. Our [review of the DHM science](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025) goes through the evidence study by study, and [DHM randomized controlled trials](/never-hungover/dhm-randomized-controlled-trials) summarizes the human trials.

For specific products, see our individual reviews of [Flyby Recovery](/never-hungover/flyby-recovery-review-2025), [Cheers Restore](/never-hungover/cheers-restore-review), [No Days Wasted](/never-hungover/no-days-wasted-dhm-review-analysis), and [Good Morning hangover pills](/never-hungover/good-morning-hangover-pills-review-2025). The products differ mainly in how much DHM is in a serving, what else is in the blend, and the price per night, which runs from $0.48 for NusaPure to $3.62 for Flyby.

## Prickly Pear: One Real Trial, Partial Benefit

Prickly pear cactus extract (Opuntia ficus indica) is one of the few hangover ingredients tested in a randomized, placebo-controlled human trial. A 2004 study in the *Archives of Internal Medicine* (Wiese and colleagues) gave volunteers prickly pear extract or placebo before drinking. The extract group reported less nausea, dry mouth, and loss of appetite, and had lower levels of an inflammation marker called C-reactive protein. However, it didn't significantly improve several other symptoms, including headache, and overall hangover severity was only modestly reduced.

That's a mixed result, but it's more than most ingredients have. It also fits the idea that inflammation plays a role in how bad a hangover feels. Prickly pear shows up in several blends, sometimes at doses much lower than the study used. We compare it head to head with DHM in [DHM vs prickly pear for hangovers](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-prickly-pear-hangovers).

## Korean and Japanese Hangover Products

Hangover drinks and pills are a huge market in South Korea and Japan. Popular products such as Condition and Dawn 808 use plant extracts, often including Hovenia dulcis, one of the plants that contains DHM, while Japan's Ukon no Chikara is built around turmeric.

The research behind these is a mix of small human studies, many from Korea, plus animal work. Some, such as studies on Hovenia fruit extract and Korean pear juice, made it into the 2022 *Addiction* review mentioned above, which found some positive results but rated the evidence very low quality. The products are popular, inexpensive, and generally considered low risk for healthy adults, but popularity isn't proof. Our full breakdown of the brands, ingredients, and what each study actually measured is in [Korean and Japanese hangover pills](/never-hungover/korean-japanese-hangover-pills).

## Probiotic Pills: ZBiotics and Myrkl

A newer category uses bacteria to break down alcohol or its by-products in the gut before they reach the bloodstream.

ZBiotics is a genetically engineered probiotic designed to make an enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde in the gut. Most acetaldehyde is made in the liver, though, and the main evidence comes from the company rather than independent trials. Our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) covers it in detail.

[Myrkl](/never-hungover/myrkl-review) is built on Bacillus bacteria, with a few added nutrients (the box lists the strains), and is sold as breaking down alcohol in the gut. A small company-backed study found lower blood alcohol in people who took it before drinking. Whether people feel better the next morning is a different question, which that study didn't answer, and independent researchers haven't repeated it.

A pill that lowers blood alcohol could also lead some people to drink more, thinking they're protected. It won't make it safe to drive, and it doesn't change your legal limit.

Opinion on both is split. On forums like Reddit, some people are enthusiastic and others say they noticed no difference and found the price hard to justify. That pattern, strong fans plus many who shrug, is what you'd expect from a product with a small real effect, a large placebo effect, or both.

## Vitamins, Electrolytes, and "Morning After" Blends

Many hangover products are mainly B vitamins, vitamin C, magnesium, zinc, and electrolytes. The logic is that drinking depletes nutrients and fluids, so topping them up should help.

There's some truth to the hydration part. Alcohol does make you urinate more, and replacing fluids helps with thirst and some headaches. But you can get most of that from water, a sports drink, or an oral rehydration solution. A few small studies have looked at B vitamins and zinc in relation to hangovers, mostly based on diet questionnaires rather than controlled trials, and the results are too weak to rely on. For a healthy person who isn't deficient, a vitamin pill after one night out is unlikely to make a noticeable difference.

If you want to get the hydration piece right, our guide on [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers timing. The same logic applies to stick-on products, which we examine in [do hangover patches work?](/never-hungover/do-hangover-patches-work).

## Activated Charcoal: One of the Weakest Options

Activated charcoal is used in hospitals for certain kinds of poisoning because it can bind some substances in the gut. That's where the hangover idea comes from. The problem is that charcoal binds alcohol very poorly, and alcohol is absorbed into the bloodstream quickly, largely from the stomach and upper small intestine. Studies in people have found that charcoal doesn't meaningfully lower blood alcohol.

Charcoal can also bind to medications and nutrients, so it can reduce the effect of other pills you take around the same time, and it can cause constipation. It's one of the weakest options in this whole category. We explain the details in [does activated charcoal help a hangover?](/never-hungover/activated-charcoal-hangover).

## Why So Many People Swear Their Pill Works

Cheers Restore has nearly 8,000 Amazon ratings averaging 4.0 stars. The reviewers aren't lying, and the gap between their experience and the trial evidence has ordinary explanations.

Headache, fatigue and "feeling rough" are exactly the symptoms that respond to expectation, so believing you've taken something useful can make you feel better. People who remember a supplement before bed also tend to drink some water, eat something or stop a little earlier, and the pill gets the credit for those habits. Hangovers also vary from night to night: the same number of drinks can leave you fine one morning and wrecked the next, depending on sleep, food and pace. Without a controlled comparison, a good morning gets credited to whatever you took.

None of this proves a product doesn't work. It explains why customer reviews can't tell you whether it does. Our [supplement reviews](/reviews) show Amazon ratings because they're useful for spotting problems like stomach upset, but we say plainly when no trial exists, and you can [compare any two products](/compare) on dose and price per serving rather than stars.

## How to Judge a Hangover Pill Before You Buy

Turn the box over and check six things.

- The label should list the exact amount of each ingredient. A "proprietary blend" hides the doses, so you can't compare the product with the research.
- The main ingredient should be close to the dose that was studied. A blend with a sprinkle of prickly pear or DHM is unlikely to do what a full study dose did.
- Third-party testing (an NSF or USP seal, or a published certificate of analysis) matters, because the FDA doesn't check supplements before sale.
- Words like "cure," "eliminate" or "drink without consequences" are red flags. Careful brands say "support" and stop there.
- Look for aspirin, acetaminophen or caffeine in the formula, since each interacts with alcohol, other medicines or health conditions.
- If you take any regular medicine, ask a pharmacist. It takes five minutes. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers the common questions.

## What Actually Works Better Than Any Pill

Every review of the evidence lands in the same place: the only reliable way to avoid a hangover is to drink less. After that, the habits with the most support cost nothing.

- Pace yourself. The body clears roughly one standard drink an hour, and drinking faster lets alcohol build up.
- Eat before and while you drink, since food slows how quickly alcohol reaches your blood.
- Alternate with water, which slows your drinking and replaces some of the fluid you lose.
- Choose clearer drinks. Vodka and gin contain fewer congeners than whiskey, brandy or red wine.
- Stop drinking a few hours before bed if you can, to protect your sleep.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through each of these in more detail. If you're already hungover, [ginger](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) has reasonable evidence for nausea in general, and food, fluids, and rest do most of the work.

## Who Should Skip Hangover Pills Entirely

Some people should avoid hangover products, or at least check with a doctor first:

- People who are **pregnant or breastfeeding**
- People with **liver or kidney disease**, or stomach ulcers
- Anyone taking **blood thinners, antidepressants, sedatives, seizure medicines, or diabetes medicines**
- Anyone with an **aspirin or NSAID allergy** (relevant for painkiller-based products)
- Anyone under the legal drinking age

If you find yourself relying on hangover pills most weekends, or you regularly feel shaky, anxious, or unwell the morning after unless you drink again, that's worth a conversation with your doctor. Those can be signs that your body is reacting to alcohol in a way a supplement can't fix.

## If You Want to Try DHM

If you still want to try a hangover supplement, DHM is the one with the most research behind it, as long as you treat it as a possible help rather than a promise. Take it with water, follow the label dose, and keep doing the basics above. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers amounts.

Two we've reviewed: [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is plain DHM, 1,000 mg a serving for $0.80. [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) adds L-cysteine and milk thistle for $1.93 a serving. Neither replaces drinking less, and neither makes it safe to drive or to mix alcohol with medicines you've been told to avoid.

## The Bottom Line

Of everything sold as a hangover pill, aspirin-based tablets are the only ones that reliably do what they say, and what they do is treat a headache. DHM has the most interesting science, mostly from animals. Prickly pear has one small human trial with partial benefit. The probiotic products rest mostly on company-funded research, none of it showing that people feel better the next day, and charcoal and vitamin packs have little to support them. Water, food, a slower pace and fewer drinks still beat anything in a bottle.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Do hangover pills actually work?**

Mostly not as well as advertised. Systematic reviews of the research published in 2005 and 2022 found no strong evidence that any pill or supplement prevents or cures hangovers. A few ingredients, including DHM, prickly pear, and some plant extracts used in Korean products, have small or early studies suggesting modest benefits for certain symptoms. Painkiller-based products can ease a headache. None of them replace drinking less.

**What is the most effective hangover pill?**

There's no clear winner, because no product has strong head-to-head trial evidence. For headache relief specifically, painkiller-based products like aspirin-and-caffeine pills tend to work, but they carry stomach risks after drinking. Among supplements, DHM has the most active research and a plausible mechanism, though human data are limited. Prickly pear has one small trial showing partial benefit.

**Are hangover pills safe?**

Most hangover supplements are generally well tolerated by healthy adults, but they aren't reviewed by the FDA for safety or effectiveness before sale. Products that contain aspirin, acetaminophen, or caffeine have real interactions with alcohol and some health conditions. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist first if you're pregnant, have liver, kidney, or stomach problems, or take any regular medication.

**Should you take hangover pills before or after drinking?**

It depends on the product. Supplements like DHM, prickly pear, and probiotic products are usually labeled for before or during drinking. Painkiller-based products are meant for the morning after, with food and water. Never take acetaminophen (Tylenol) before or while drinking to prevent a hangover, because the combination can stress the liver.

**Does Blowfish work for hangovers?**

Blowfish combines aspirin and caffeine, so it does ease a hangover headache and grogginess, much like a standard headache tablet with coffee. It doesn't address the underlying causes of a hangover. Because aspirin can irritate the stomach and raise bleeding risk, especially after drinking, it isn't suitable for people with ulcers, those on blood thinners, or anyone told to avoid aspirin.

**Does activated charcoal prevent hangovers?**

There's no good evidence that it does. Activated charcoal binds alcohol poorly, and alcohol is absorbed into the bloodstream quickly. Studies in people found that charcoal doesn't meaningfully lower blood alcohol. It can also interfere with medications taken around the same time.

**Why do so many people say hangover pills work for them?**

Hangover symptoms are subjective and vary a lot from night to night, so the placebo effect is strong. People who remember to take a pill also tend to drink water, eat, or stop earlier, and the pill gets the credit. That doesn't mean every product is useless. It means customer reviews can't tell you whether a product works, which is why controlled trials matter.
